"When Allah intends evil for a servant, He appoints for him a devil before his death (p-177), so he sees nothing good except that he makes it ugly to him, and nothing ugly except that he makes it good in his sight."

And Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Abu Ya'la, and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih narrated from 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah intends good for the governor, He makes for him a minister of truth: if he forgets, he reminds him, and if he remembers, he helps him. And if He intends otherwise for him, He makes for him a minister of evil: if he forgets, he does not remind him, and if he remembers, he does not help him."

Al-Bukhari narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with them both), and al-Nasa'i from Abu Hurayrah alone (may Allah be pleased with him), and al-Bukhari also from Abu Ayyub (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah never sent a prophet nor appointed a caliph except that he had an inner circle (*bitana*) that commanded him to good and urged him toward it, and an inner circle that commanded him to evil and urged him toward it. The one protected is he whom Allah protects."

In al-Nasa'i's narration: "There is no governor except that he has two inner circles: an inner circle that commands him to good and forbids him from evil, and an inner circle that does not spare him corruption. Whoever is protected from the evil of the latter has indeed been protected [and he is with whichever of the two overcomes him]." The narration of al-Bukhari from Abu Ayyub is similar to it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 26:

When He informed of their loss, He indicated it by what He coordinated with what the context guided to in its implied estimate from His words: "So they turned away" – i.e., these Arabs – "and said" – this was the original form, but He said instead, drawing attention to the attribute that necessitated their turning away: ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾ – i.e., they concealed what their intellects pointed them to of the truth – ﴿Do not listen﴾ – i.e., anything at all of listening in general – ﴿to this Qur'an﴾ – specifying it by a demonstrative, to exclude other ancient books such as the Torah. Al-Qushayri said: "Because it overpowers hearts and seizes intellects, and everyone who listens to it inclines towards it." ﴿And make noise﴾ [i.e., engage in idle talk] from laghiya – with kasra, yalghā – with fatha – when one speaks with what has no benefit [in it] ﴿therein﴾, i.e., make it a vessel for noise, by being excessive in nonsense, delirium and idle chatter, with whistling and clapping – i.e., the whistling and clapping and other things – while it is being recited, so that its reciter falls into error and mistake. Al-Qushayri said: "They said this without knowing that whoever has his heart illuminated with faith, is strengthened with understanding, is supplied with insight, and is granted the unveiling of hearing the secret from the Unseen, it is he who hears and believes, while he who is in the darkness of his ignorance, faith does not enter his heart, and hearing does not reach his secret."

﴿So that you may prevail﴾ – i.e., so that your state becomes that of one who is hoped to overcome and attain his aim, in that someone inclines towards him, or falls silent, or forgets what he was saying. This indicates that they knew that whoever hears it without a desire of his own inclines towards it and turns entirely to it. They exposed themselves by this with a disgrace unlike any other, for they were challenged to produce something like it so that they might be counted as victors, and they found nothing by which they could hope for victory except whistling, clapping and similar idle noise in opposition to what rises above the highest peaks of speech, to a point where there is no hope or aspiration. What they produced conveys no meaning except that they are incapable of opposition, and are certain that whenever they produce anything of it they will be disgraced; and everyone who heard it was certain that they were defeated.

When they deserved this punishment, He stated the consequence of that, emphasizing their denial of His words, the Exalted: ﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste a severe punishment﴾. He stated the apparent noun in place of the pronoun to generalize by the attribute, saying ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, meaning: these and others. ﴿A severe punishment﴾ in this world through deprivation and the various kinds of humiliation that follow it, and in the Hereafter through the Fires. ﴿And We will surely recompense them﴾, meaning: for their deeds. Since He who is able to do the more severe is able to do what is less than it, He said: ﴿the worst﴾, meaning: the recompense of the worst deed ﴿that they used to do﴾, with it being for them like instincts (gharaʾiz, innate dispositions), ﴿persistently﴾ (muwaẓibīn) engaged in it.

(p-180) When He, glory be to Him, had gone to the utmost in warning against their punishment, He increased in glorifying Himself and in His grace toward whoever among His servants He wished to guide, and in establishing proof against others. So He said: ﴿That﴾, meaning the recompense that is the worst, very great indeed, ﴿is the recompense of﴾. Since the enmity of one who cannot be overcome is an exceptionally great matter, he drew attention to this by turning the speech away from the manifest form of it to something greater than it, and so said: ﴿the enemies of Allah﴾, meaning the Greatest King. This is because they did not do anything less than the worst except through incapacity to do so, since their innate disposition (jibilla) requires it. He explained this by His words: ﴿the Fire﴾, and specified some of what is in it by His words: ﴿for them in it﴾, meaning in the Fire, ﴿is the abode of eternity﴾, meaning the place that surrounds them and encircles them, without any knowledge of it from a corner or otherwise by which the specific location within it could be identified, together with its announcement of permanence, constancy, and the impossibility of separation. Or it is in an abstract sense, meaning: for them it is an abode of eternity, just as they had in the world an abode of pleasure, in the sense that it itself was for them an abode of amusement and deception.

Since they were, in their deeds for which they deserved this punishment, persisting with a persistence that makes their separation from it impossible, He increased the goodness of His words: ﴿recompense﴾, that is, a requital in exact correspondence, ﴿for what they were﴾, that is, by innate disposition and nature, and He returned the speech to the manifest form of greatness that calls for retribution, so He said: ﴿for denying Our signs﴾, meaning in accordance with their greatness, ﴿they used to deny﴾, meaning they rejected them out of obstinacy, without regard for their exaltedness in themselves or their exaltedness by their attribution to Us. Because of their denial, they would engage in what no rational person would approve of, such as frivolity and other things.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 29:

When it became clear to them that what had brought upon them this evil was that their skins bore witness against them, and their companions (quranaa') had led them astray, and mutual hatred and enmity had arisen among all of them, so that each one's wish for the other's evil became an increase in their punishment, and the harm done to their skins was their own harm, they singled out their companions for the desire to take revenge upon them. Then He, glory be to Him, related their statement with His words, in conjunction with ﴿And they say to their skins﴾ [Fussilat: 21], or in connection with what is implied, namely: then they knew at that time that they had been upon error, due to their negligence in reflection and their blind following of others: ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, i.e., they covered the lights of their intellects, calling upon [something] that, if it could hear them, would not respond; so it is an increase in their punishment. His relating it to us is an admonition and a warning: ﴿Our Lord﴾, i.e., O You who never once cut off Your kindness from us, ﴿show us﴾ the two categories ﴿who led us astray﴾ from the path that leads to the place of good pleasure ﴿of the jinn and mankind﴾ who adorned for us the commission of evil, secretly and openly. The majority of reciters read the ra' in "arinaa" with a kasra; Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Ya'qub, and al-Susi from Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it with a sukun on the ra' here specifically.

Al-Asbahani said: It is related from al-Khalil that if you say "arini thawbaka" with a kasra, the meaning is "make me see it," and if you say it with a sukun, it is a request for giving, meaning "give me your garment." Its parallel is the common usage of ita' in the meaning of i'ta' (giving), while its original meaning is "bringing into presence" — end of quotation.

﴿We will place them beneath our feet﴾ in the Fire, as a humiliation to them, just as they placed us beneath their command, ﴿so that they may be among the lowest﴾, i.e., among the people of the lowest rank of the Fire and among those who are beneath us, just as they made us so in the world in reality, by our following them in what they intended against us, and in the Hereafter by this condition. The apparent meaning is that each person wishes to know who led him astray from the two categories, so that he may do that to them, if he is able to do so.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 30:

When he had mentioned the enemies and their companions as a warning, he followed it with the mention of the allies and their companions as good news. He said, clarifying their state, which is susceptible to turning away and to its fruits, as an answer to one who asks about them, emphasizing it to counter the obstinate deniers: ﴿Indeed, those who﴾. Abu Hayyan (Abu Hayyan al-Andalusi) said: Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: it was revealed concerning al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him and content him).

﴿say﴾, that is, a true utterance, convinced of it in the heart and articulated by the tongue, affirming the caller of Allah in the abode of this world, humbling themselves where humility benefits, combining the foundation, which is knowledge (ma'rifah) and belief (i'tiqad), and the building, which is righteous deed by word and action, upon rectitude. The root of the perfections of the soul is a corrective certainty and a righteous deed: you know the truth for its own sake and the good in order to act upon it. The head of certain knowledge and its chief is the knowledge of Allah, and the head of righteous deeds is steadfastness upon the limit of moderation, without inclining toward either extreme of excess or deficiency: ﴿Our Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to us, ﴿is Allah﴾, the One specified with majesty and honor, alone, without partner.

(p-183) Since remaining steadfast upon monotheism (tawhid) and what sustains it until death is a matter of lofty rank that is not attained except by the granting of success from the One of majesty and honor, he indicated this with the particle of delay, saying: ﴿then they became steadfast﴾, they sought and established the upright standing (qiwam) in faith in all the messengers and all the books. They did not associate with Him an idol, nor an image, nor a human, nor an angel, nor a star, nor anything else in worship or in show-off, and they acted in what pleases Him and avoided everything that angers Him, however long the time, in compliance with what He commanded at the beginning of the surah in His saying: ﴿Indeed your God is one God, so go straight to Him﴾ [Fussilat: 6]. Whoever has the root of steadfastness in tawhid is safe from the Fire by not abiding in it, and whoever has the perfection of steadfastness in the fundamentals and the branches is safe from the threat. ﴿The angels descend﴾ by way of continuous gradualness, ﴿upon them﴾ from the moment He breathed the spirit into them until they die, and then until they enter Paradise, inwardly and outwardly, ﴿the angels﴾, with support in all that befalls them, so the angelic states prevail over their human attributes and their animal appetites, and these dissolve before them, and their inner mirrors (marai) are illuminated. Then he explained the support with which they are strengthened and interpreted it, saying: ﴿Do not fear﴾, that is, of anything similar that frightens, and it is as though they are fixing that in their hearts. ﴿Nor grieve﴾, that is, over anything that has escaped you, for what has been attained for you is better than it, so your times in the Hereafter (p-184) are in it; rather, all of them are spirit and comfort, so nothing desired escapes them for that reason, and nothing disliked reaches them. ﴿And rejoice﴾, that is, fill your breasts with joy whose effect appears on your skin by the radiance of the face and the delight of the whole body, ﴿in the Garden which you were﴾, that is, a great reality, through the tongues of the messengers, ﴿promised﴾, that is, that this will be renewed for you at every moment through the books and the messengers. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': they are given good news in three places: at death, in the grave, and on the Day of Resurrection, and that is the end of the quotation. This is to be understood as a reference to the true speech, and what precedes it is to be understood as meaning that they do with it what I have translated.

This is the commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 31.

When they established good for them and negated harm from them, they gave the reason for this in their saying: ﴿We are your allies﴾, meaning, the nearest of the close relatives to you. So we do with you everything that a close relative can do ﴿in the life of this world﴾. We bring you delights, keep harms far from you, and carry you toward all goods, such that you will have in them what the intellects prefer, through abstaining from what the souls desire, even if it appears to onlookers in this world that the matter is the opposite of that. So we wake you from sleep, carry you to prayer and fasting, and keep you far from sins, the opposite of what the devils do with their allies. ﴿And in the Hereafter﴾ likewise, where friends become enemies to one another except the God-fearing. ﴿And for you therein﴾, that is, in the Hereafter, in the Garden and before entering it, throughout all the times of the Gathering, ﴿is whatever you desire﴾ (p-185) even at the lowest degrees of desire, as indicated by the omission of the object, ﴿your souls﴾, because of what you restrained them from desires in this world. ﴿And for you﴾

Since the context concerns those who stood firm, which is general to the foremost (al-sabiqun) and the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin), and as was indicated, the closing is with the attribute of forgiveness and its placement first, he restricted it with the adverbial phrase, unlike what is in Ya-Sin. So he said: ﴿therein﴾, that is, in the Hereafter, ﴿is whatever you ask for﴾, that is, whatever you prefer to call for, request, seek from Him, and wish for by the desire of your souls and the eagerness of your hearts.

When this whole matter is compared with what they are given, it is only a small thing, so He drew attention to it by His saying: ﴿nuzulan﴾ (a welcome gift), meaning: all of this will be yours, just as a guest is provided for upon his arrival until what he is to be hosted with is made ready. And since whoever is called to account is punished, no one enters Paradise except by mercy, He indicated this by His saying: ﴿min﴾ (from), meaning: the welcome gift comes from ﴿Ghafur﴾ (Most Forgiving), who possesses the attribute of erasing sins, both their essence and their effect, to a degree that cannot be described, ﴿Rahim﴾ (Most Merciful), meaning: abundant in mercy with what the Divine Majesty is pleased with. The summary is that the one who corrupts himself, God assigns to him companions of evil from among the jinn and mankind, who increase him in corruption; and the one who reforms himself, God makes easy for him friends of goodness from among mankind and the angels, who guide him, make him love all good things, and keep him away from and make him hate all harmful things. And God takes charge of the righteous.

[p. 186] Since this applies to one who perfects himself, he follows it with one who perfects others, indicating that complete happiness is for a person to acquire virtuous qualities through which he becomes perfect in himself. When he has finished, he occupies himself with perfecting the deficient, coordinating it with what is implied: "How excellent is this one who has perfected himself." He said this to highlight the high rank of beneficial action that extends to others, and to urge persistence in calling people, even if they refuse and say, ﴿Our hearts are under coverings﴾ [Fussilat: 5], then say, ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an﴾ [Fussilat: 26]. Whenever they said anything of that sort, its sufficient and healing answers were mentioned, so all doubts were dispelled and the darkness of misguidance vanished. Thus the warning against calling becomes a place of acceptance. ﴿And who is better in speech﴾, meaning in terms of speech, ﴿than one who calls﴾, and the singular form of the pronoun indicates the rarity of this category, ﴿to Allah﴾, meaning the One whose perfect qualities encompass all creation, so he entreats every person through the attributes by which He, glorified is He, has made Himself known. ﴿And does﴾, meaning while he has actually done, ﴿righteousness﴾ within himself, so that this makes his calling more effective. This is general, whether it is good intention, speech, or actions of the outward limbs, done secretly or openly. For this reason the qualified noun was omitted, lest it imply that it is restricted to outward deeds, and because "called" (da'a) is sufficient in itself. This differs from contexts concerned with repentance, such as the verse in al-Furqan, or with belief in resurrection, such as the verse in al-Kahf, where outward action must be shown to serve as evidence of the soundness of belief and the completeness of repentance. Here, the calling itself suffices for that. ﴿And he said﴾, emphasizing (p. 187) to the opponent and the friend alike, and cutting off the hope of the corrupter regarding him: ﴿Indeed, I am of the Muslims﴾, meaning those firmly established in the attribute of Islam, openly declaring it and not fearing the blame of any blamer in the matter of Allah, even if the people of his time call him such-and-such, rough, harsh, or stubborn, because of his firmness in opposing them in what they are upon, and his readiness to submit to everything his Lord, glorified is He, has commanded him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 34:

When the implied sense was: no one is better in speech than he, rather He alone is the Doer of good, so this doer and others are not at all equal, as a refutation of them (the idea) that their state is better than the state of those who call to Allah, and since carrying out the perfecting of creation requires a great inner struggle (jihad al-nafs) of bearing hardships and patience over harm, and other than that of all the (moral) qualities, He joined to it the distinction between their two deeds, as an encouragement toward good deeds, and said: ﴿And not equal﴾, that is, even if you strive in examination and reflection, ﴿the good deed﴾, that is, not in relation to the individual members of its kind, nor in relation to its doers when it is alone, because good deeds differ in themselves, and a single good deed differs according to the intentions of those who do it and their striving in it, nor in relation to other than it. Pointing to this is the emphasis in His saying: ﴿nor the bad deed﴾, that is, in itself, nor in relation to another kind.

When this produced the exhortation to turn toward goodness and turn away from evil, and made clear that each of the two categories varies in its particulars and in its levels of rank, and since a person is never free of accidents that befall him from people and from himself, requiring him to repel some of them, He produced, at the aim of the highest, and said: ﴿Repel﴾, that is, everything that can harm you from yourself and from people, ﴿with that which is better﴾, that is, the qualities and states which are, as far as possible, the best of righteous deeds. So pardoning the wrongdoer is good, and doing good to him is better than that. ﴿Then, behold, he between whom and you there is enmity﴾, a great enmity that has filled what lies between the two, will suddenly be, in his condition, ﴿as though he were a close friend﴾, that is, near, doing what a near one does, ﴿a warm friend﴾, that is, in the utmost nearness, leaving no matter of importance unfulfilled except that he settles it, facilitates it, eases it, cures his ailments, brings near what is distant, and removes his filth, just as hot water removes dirt.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 35:

Since this trait is a comprehensive mother (umm jami') of all the benefits of the religion and the world, he said, drawing attention to its great excellence and wondrous nobility, urging people to take shelter in the whole of its shade, and indicating by the passive voice that it is the principal aim intended in itself, in a manner that alerts to its being contrary to the natural disposition of man, as an incitement to desire it from its Giver (p-189): ﴿And none is granted it﴾, meaning, none is made to meet this trait, which is the return of evil with the best of good, namely ihsan (doing good), which is better than pardon, forbearance, patience and tolerance, by God Most High fixing His will, with intensity and emphasis, on bestowing it upon him. ﴿Except those who are patient﴾, meaning, this reality has come into existence among them and has taken root in their natures, so they come to suppress their rage and bear with what is hateful. He repeated the passive form for the sake of alerting that there is no capacity for it at all except through the Creator's granting of success, by a sort of innate matter (amr watani) that God casts into the heart as a casting of inspiration, whose fruit shows across the whole body. So he said, using the repetition of the negative to indicate greater magnitude, and to indicate that the people of this trait are of two ranks, each rank being intended in itself: ﴿And none is granted it﴾ with all the greatness it has ﴿except﴾ (he used the singular here after the plural of "those who are patient" to indicate the rarity of one who is steadfast in this trait) ﴿one who has a great portion﴾, meaning a share, a lot and a fortune, ﴿great﴾, meaning sublime, in this world and the Hereafter, with God and with people.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 36:

Since the implied sense is: "If you encounter that, and Allah protects you from Satan, then you are [still] you," he joined to it his words, expressing it with the particle of doubt (in-ta'bīr bi-adāt al-shakk), which conveys the possibility of such an occurrence in general, even though it is known that he (ﷺ) is protected from sin (ma'sūm). This points to the rank of the human being insofar as he is human, and to the fact that Satan, despite knowing that he is protected, imagines that he is able to do that, and so he hangs his hope upon it. It seems that for this reason it was emphasized, because his prodding of him is in the place of denial: ﴿wa-immā﴾ ("and if"). And since the whisperings of Satan stir one toward what is not fitting (lā yanbaghī), and the intelligent person does not do what is not fitting except under compulsion, he likened the one who is incited by it to one who is goaded, whom the goad drives to commit what harms him. So he said: ﴿yanzaghannaka﴾, meaning: it goads you and stabs you with a corrupting stab, so that you feel pain, ﴿min al-shayṭān﴾ ("from Satan"), the one far from mercy, burned by the curse. And since the situation was dangerous, because the natural disposition (al-ṭab') assists the whispering, he made the prodding itself a prodder, as a sign of that, and said: ﴿nazgh﴾, meaning: a whisper that moves toward the one whispered to, on account of which it is moved, and sends him forth as one goaded is sent toward the direction in which he is driven, so if he is driven in that direction with great resolve, ﴿fa-ista'iudh bi-Allāh﴾, meaning: seek refuge with the Sovereign Most High, and ask Him to enter you into His protection, hastening to that at the moment you are pricked by the prod, for none other than Him can grant refuge from it. And do not let the prod repeat itself; rather, return to the One encompassing in knowledge and power at the first thought (awwal al-khaṭra), for if you do not oppose the first thought, it becomes a reflection (fikra), so resolve arises, then the slip occurs, then it becomes hardness of heart (qaswa), so persistence (tamādī) follows. This was noted by al-Qushayrī.

Since seeking refuge here is from Satan, and his prodding is something known and not seen, and the attribute of hearing is the attribute of what is seen and what is not seen, he said, emphasizing against the stance of those who stop at the outward appearances: ﴿innahu huwa﴾, meaning: He alone is ﴿al-Samī'u﴾ ("the All-Hearing"), and he concluded with His words: ﴿al-'Alīm﴾ ("the All-Knowing"), who hears every thing heard, from your seeking refuge and from other things, and knows every thing known, from his prodding and from other things. So He is the One able to repel his plot and weaken his affair and strengthen you against it, and He is not like what you have made for Him of equals, the deaf and mute, who have no power over anything at all.

When he had mentioned that they assign rivals to Him, although He created the earth in two days, and concluded that the best of goodness is calling to Allah, and concluded the matter with a call through the attribute of knowledge, he followed it with the proofs of monotheism, to inform that monotheism is the best of goodness, which drives out everything else, and to alert that calling to Allah the Exalted is an expression for illuminating the proofs that indicate the Essence and the Attributes. This is done by explaining the acts and their effects, and He is the one who knows everything in it of parts and components, substance (jawhar) and accident ('arad). He began with mention of the celestial matters because they are more indicative. He said, conjoining it to what is implied: ﴿And of His signs﴾, which arise from the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, which entails the comprehensiveness of His power, which produces His restoring of whomever He wills, and the penetration of His disposal over everything He wills, which entails His singularity in divinity: that He created the two regions, as has passed, in six days: ﴿And of His signs﴾, which indicate His oneness:

*In everything there is for Him a sign*
*That indicates that He is the One.*

Since darkness is non-existence and light is existence, and non-existence is prior, He said: ﴿the night and the day﴾, meaning, the two that indicate by their alternation and their states His power over (p-192) resurrection and over every possible thing. ﴿And the sun and the moon﴾, which are the night and the day, like the spirit to bodies. These existents, together with what has passed of the creation of the two regions, are the book of the King, the Judge, addressed to humans and jinn, witnessed by them through direct sight, as it has been said: O human,

*Contemplate the lines of existent things, for they*
*Are messages to you from the Most High King.*

*In them He has inscribed, if you contemplate, a script,*
*Everything except Allah is vanity.*

Since His glory's singularity in creation and command was established, and He is hidden except through the light of Allah, or the sun and the moon were among His known signs, pointing to Him in the existence of this world and the next, and they were observable, and man is of limited intellect, his imagination bound to what is observed because of the preoccupations he has, except those whom Allah protects, He produced His saying, warning against worshipping them, because of the splendor seen in them and the benefits in them: ﴿Do not prostrate to the sun﴾, which is the greatest of your idols, for it is among His originated creations. He repeated the negation for emphasis, and to convey that the prohibition concerns each of them separately. For this reason he placed the explicit noun in the position of the pronoun, saying: ﴿nor to the moon﴾, likewise.

When He forbade prostration to them, He commanded prostration to the one whose worthiness of it (p-193) is shown, and the lack of worthiness in them or the worthiness of something other than them, saying: ﴿but prostrate﴾, and He drew attention to His greater majesty by placing the explicit name in the position of the pronoun, saying: ﴿to Allah﴾, meaning the One who possesses every perfection, without any flaw of deficiency, of change or renewal of states, ﴿who created them﴾, meaning the four, for your sake. He is the one who deserves divinity. He used the feminine because what does not reason takes the grammatical rule of the feminine in pronouns, and they are also signs. In this is an indication of the extreme lowliness of these things compared to what they were made worthy of, and a censure of their worshippers for extreme foolishness. It is possible that counting the moon as moons is because it is sometimes a crescent, sometimes a full moon, and sometimes it disappears; therefore He used the plural, indicating His subjugation of the two by change in its body and by making them move. For this reason He expressed it with the feminine pronoun, which is used for the plural of multitude of non-rational things.

When it became clear that all are His servants, and a master does not accept his servant associating another servant in the worship of his master, He said: ﴿If you are indeed He alone you worship﴾, meaning, specifically, with utmost firmness, ﴿as is the plain sense of your saying in supplication in times of hardship, especially at sea﴾. The sum of your statement is: ﴿We do not worship them except that they bring us near to Allah in position﴾ [az-Zumar: 3]. So if you associate anything with Him in prostration or otherwise, you have not singled Him out for worship, because prostration (p-194) is part of worship, and performing it for another, even at one time, is association in general. Whoever associates with Him has not worshipped Him alone, and whoever does not worship Him alone has not worshipped Him at all, for He is the most self-sufficient of the self-sufficient; He accepts only the sincere, and He is nearer to His servants than anything, so He is about to take vengeance for your association. In the verse there is an indication of encouraging the safeguarding of human beings against performing prostration to other than Him, elevating their station above prostrating to a creature after they were made those to whom prostration is done. For He, glory be to Him, commanded the angels, who are the noblest of His creation after them, to prostrate to Adam while they were in his loins, and Iblis the accursed became arrogant. So curse him. How far apart are the two stations.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 38:

Since they were, in this matter, between obedience and disobedience, and the averting of corruptions (dar' al-mafasid) takes precedence, he made this the cause (sabbaba 'an dhalika) of his saying, expressing it with the particle of doubt (bi-adatil-shakk) as an alert to them that their arrogance after the establishment of these proofs should not be presumed; and he turned the speech to the third person (al-ghayba) to belittle them and distance them, on the assumption that this occurs from them: ﴿So if they are arrogant﴾, that is, they produce arrogance toward following you in what I commanded them of tawhid, so they did not affirm God as one, nor did they declare Him exalted above partners. ﴿Then those who are with﴾ and he made manifest the place of concealment (al-isjar), expressing it with the attribute of goodness as glad tidings to him and warning to them: ﴿your Lord﴾, specifically, not "with them," because they are brought near to Him in the rank of good pleasure and honor, and because they are of those whom the children of Adam are absorbed in (yastaghriqu bihi al-adamiyyun), and because the disbelievers have no power to reach them in any way: ﴿glorify Him﴾, that is, they perform the declaring Him free from deficiencies and keep far from association, because of His supreme holiness and greatest might, not for anything other than Him, sincerely in His worship, and they are not arrogant.

Since the state of the disbelievers in sincerity varies in hardship and ease, he pointed to the reprehensibility of that in them by generalizing its specific property, upon them be prayer and peace, to sincerity in the two states: affirmation, which is a state of expansion in general, and effacement, which is a state of contraction likewise. They renew this declaring Him free (tanzih) continually in every time, so he said: ﴿by night and day﴾, that is, over the passing of the two alternations and the return of the two renewals, they never slacken. And since it was within the context of the reproach for their arrogance, which requires their denial, he emphasized with the conjunction and the pronoun, saying, signaling that this is their constant practice from which they never part: ﴿and they﴾, that is, and the state being that they are in this constancy, ﴿do not tire﴾, that is, there is hardly any slackening or weariness for them at any time. He is therefore free of the worship of these people, indeed free of the worship of every worshipper, and the greater share belongs to the one who has Him; as for Him, subhanahu, He gains nothing by it and nothing diminishes Him. So leave these people, "if they are arrogant," and their affair, and they will know who the loser is. The verse is of the type of ihtibak: he mentioned arrogance first as an indication of its omission second, and glorification second as an indication of its omission first; and the secret of that is that he mentioned the most reprehensible of what belongs to His enemies and the most excellent of what belongs to His friends.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 39:

When He mentioned some of the signs of the heavens, for their nobility, and because some of them have been worshipped, and they are among the traces of divinity, and He mentioned their indication of His oneness, from which the nullification of their worship necessarily follows, He followed it with some of the signs of the earth, unlike what is in Ya-Sin, for the context there concerns resurrection and the signs of the earth are more indicative. So He said: ﴿And among His signs﴾, meaning, those that indicate the greatness of His affair and the loftiness of His dominion, ﴿that you see the earth﴾, meaning, some of it with the sense of sight, and some of it with the eye of insight, by analogy to what it has seen, because all of it is equal in relation to power.

Since the context concerns oneness, He expressed it with what is closer to the state of the worshipper, unlike what passed in al-Hajj, so He said: ﴿humbled﴾, meaning, dry, with no vegetation in it, so it is in the form of the abject one who has no protection, for there is no barrier to walking upon it, since it is level after covering its face, unlike when it is stirring, swelling, adorned, showing off with vegetation. (p-197) Since the sending down of water is among what He, glorified be He, has singled Himself out with, and it is among the greatest proofs of the greatness of the One, He turned the speech to the locus of greatness, so He said: ﴿So when We send down﴾, by what We possess of complete power and greatness, ﴿upon it water﴾, from the clouds, or We drive it to it from high places, and We bring with it from the mud what makes it fit for vegetation, even if it is saline like the land of Egypt, ﴿it stirs﴾, meaning, it moves with a great, abundant, swift movement, so it is like one who is laboring at that by himself, ﴿and swells﴾, meaning, it splits open, so its dust rises, the vegetation emerges from it, rises into the air covering its face, its roots branch out, and its stalks thicken, so it prevents passage over it as it was in its former ease, and by the beauty of its adornment it becomes like one who struts in lush garments after having been naked and abject in worn rags and a wretched state. Likewise hearts, when they are humbled by sensing what sins have afflicted them, the Truth, glorified be He, turns toward them and purifies them with the waters of knowledge, so the blessings of regret appear in them, He pardons their owners for what they fell short of in sincere steadfastness, they shine with the adornment of acts of obedience, take pride in the garments of acts of nearness, and are purified by the varieties of manifestations.

Since this is a visible proof of the power to bring the non-existent into being and restore the decayed and crumbled, it necessarily produces His saying, emphasizing it because of their denial, turning the speech away from the locus of greatness to what alerts to the power over resurrection, necessarily: (p-198) ﴿Indeed, He who revives it﴾, by what He brought forth of its vegetation, which had been decayed and crushed and had become dust, ﴿is surely the Reviver of the dead﴾, just as He did with the vegetation, without any difference. And since they, despite their acknowledgment of His complete power, were as if they denied His power by their denial of resurrection, He said, giving the reason and emphasizing: ﴿Indeed, He is over all things Competent﴾, because possibilities are equal in their standing in relation to power, so whoever is perfectly capable of one of them is capable of the others.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 40:

When he had explained that the call to God is the greatest of positions and the most noble of ranks, and explained that it is only attained through clarifying the proofs of tawhid (divine unity), of which the greatest is the resurrection, and he explained it to such a degree of clarity, the threat became sufficient for whoever turned away from accepting it. So he said, in a general expression directed to him and to others, emphasizing as a warning that their action is the action of one who thinks that He, glory be to Him, does not perceive their deeds: ﴿Indeed, those who distort﴾ meaning, those who incline, diverting the meanings away from the intended purpose and the paths of justice, such as their saying ﴿We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to God in position﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], or who create confusion through idle talk, through whistling and clapping and other kinds of noise and clamor, and everything that is encompassed by the meaning of inclination away from what its intention may rightly be.

Since daring to commit distortion (ilhad) undermines acknowledgment of greatness, He repeated the manifestation of it, saying: ﴿in Our signs﴾, in light of the greatness they possess, which indicates what belongs to Us of oneness, comprehensiveness of knowledge, and perfection of power. Since knowledge of the wrongdoing together with power is the cause of seizure, He said, establishing knowledge after establishing power: ﴿are not hidden from Us﴾, meaning at no time and in no respect, while We are able to seize them; whenever We will, We seize. Hastening is only done by one deficient, who fears missing out.

Since distortion is the cause of casting its perpetrator into the Fire, and the implied meaning is: "We are forbearing toward the disobedient; whoever returns to Us is secure from every fear, and whoever persists in turning away until death, We cast into the Fire," He made His saying, exalted is He, a consequence of this: ﴿Is one who is cast into the Fire﴾, meaning, on his face, with the easiest of matters, because of his distortion in the signs and his turning away from the clear proofs, so he will be fearful on the Day of Resurrection because of what he sees of the preliminaries of that, until what he feared overtakes him ﴿better, or one who comes﴾ to Us ﴿secure on the Day of Resurrection﴾, when We gather Our servants for presentation before Us for judgment among them with justice, so he enters Paradise, the abode of peace, and his security endures. The verse is of ihtibak: He mentioned casting into the Fire first as an indication of entering Paradise second, and security second as an indication of fear first. Its secret is that He mentioned the intended purpose in itself, which is that for which fear occurred, first, and security, which is in reality living, second.

Since this is a sufficient deterrent, and the intelligent person must inevitably turn from evil deeds to goodness, hoping for God's bounty and grace, He produced His saying, threatening, warning and promising punishment, turning the speech from the third person to the second person because it is more indicative of anger at persistence after this clarification: ﴿Do what you will﴾, meaning, you have known the fate of the wrongdoer and the doer of good, so whoever wishes any of the two recompenses, let him perform his deeds, for he will certainly meet it. Since the doer does not hope for neglect except on the assumption that deeds are hidden, and the one for whom action is done does not leave off recompense except out of ignorance or incapacity, He explained that He, glory be to Him, is all-encompassing in knowledge, knowing the weight of the smallest atom, so He said, encouraging, deterring, and emphasizing, because they act like one who thinks that their deeds are concealed, turning away from the manifestation of greatness to what is most indicative of singularity, lest one think that increased knowledge comes through many means: ﴿Indeed, He﴾, and He placed their deeds first as a notice of extreme concern with their matter, saying: ﴿of what you do﴾, meaning at every time, ﴿is Seeing﴾, seeing with sight and knowledge; so He is, over everything, among you, Powerful.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 41:

When He made the choice in action (al-ikhtiyar fi al-'amal) a threat to them, He followed it with information about what awaits those who oppose it. He said, emphasizing to deny their doubts about the contents over which the emphasis (al-ta'kid) has entered: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved﴾, that is, those who concealed the clear signs of the intellects that point to the truth, denying (mukadhdhibin) ﴿the Reminder﴾ which, in reality, has no other reminder ﴿when it came to them﴾ without any hesitation at all, and this indicates from them the utmost obstinacy. ﴿And indeed it﴾, that is, while the fact is that it is ﴿a Book﴾, that is, one comprising every good, ﴿mighty﴾, that is, there is none like it, so it overcomes every reminder and no reminder overcomes it nor comes near it, and it defeats every opponent, and no opponent can ever prevail over it in overthrowing it.

When [the Qur'an] had among the meanings of its might (ʿizza) that it is protected, by the solidity of its composition, the eloquence of its arrangement, and the sublimity of its meanings, from any alteration whatsoever, he clarified this with His saying: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it﴾, meaning: falsehood that is clearly false cannot come upon it, so that it would become, or any part of it would become, manifestly false. Since the intended meaning is the generalization of the negation, and not the negation of generality, he introduced the prepositional phrase and said: ﴿from before it or behind it﴾. That is, from the direction of the outward (ẓāhir), like what He commanded, He informed of concerning what came before it. ﴿Nor from behind it﴾ means from the direction of the inward knowledge (ʿilm bāṭin), like the knowledge of what has not become well known of what exists and what is yet to come, whether it be a ruling or a report, because it is in the utmost degree of truth and veracity. The sum is that it cannot approach it from any of the directions, because what is in front is the most evident of things, and what is behind is the most hidden of things, so what lies between these is all the more so. The expression is thus a metaphor (kināya) for that, because the attributes of God have, in reality, neither a behind nor a front. Likewise, there is no beyond God a target, nor beneath God a limit, and similar expressions that the Arabs understand, and from the knowledge of their language, (p. 202) their intended meaning without ambiguity. Then he gave the reason for that with His saying: ﴿A revelation﴾, meaning gradually, according to what serves the interests, ﴿from One who is All-Wise﴾, possessed of perfect wisdom, so He places each thing in it in its most fitting place at the time of its revelation and within the context of the composition, ﴿Praiseworthy﴾, meaning one who fully encompasses the attributes of perfection, of wisdom and others, and of transcendence, purity, and holiness above every trace of deficiency. Every creature praises Him with the tongue of its state, even if it does not praise Him with a spoken tongue, through what becomes apparent in it of its deficiency or its perfection. The predicate is elided, its estimated form being: "they will certainly be losers," because they cannot prevail over anything of what they direct toward it of criticism, since they are weak, feeble, and small, as al-Maʿarri said:

I see the Pleiades (al-Jawzāʾ) too great to be hunted,
so wage enmity against whom you are able to oppose in enmity.

Omitting the predicate is more awe-inspiring, so that the soul may go every way.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 43:

When He described the Remembrance (dhikr) as something that is not corrupted and whose imperfection cannot be conceived of reaching it, and so the claim of those who said ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during its recitation﴾ [Fussilat: 26] and similar things that have passed were nullified and safety from them was secured, He followed this with consolation for what the Prophet might suffer of distress. This is so that patience may be exercised in the face of all their sayings. So He said: ﴿What is said to you﴾, meaning: what is brought into existence against you, whether it was in past time, present time, or future, from any of the disbelievers or others, by which there results constriction of the breast or disturbance of thought, such as their saying ﴿Our hearts are under coverings from what you call us to﴾ [Fussilat: 5], to the end of it. And other than that, of what has preceded, that they said it to him (p-203) while seeking to trouble him. ﴿Except what﴾, meaning: nothing, ﴿has been said﴾, meaning: his words have come to be in that manner, ﴿to the messengers﴾. Even if it was not said to each one of them individually, it was said to the group collectively. And it is alerted that this was not for [a period] encompassing all time, but at times and at other times, by the inclusion of the preposition in His saying ﴿before you﴾.

When by this statement the intended consolation was achieved, the expectation for them would have been that there would befall them what had befallen the nations before them of the punishment of annihilation. The Prophet (ﷺ) was intensely compassionate toward them and eager for their betterment, so He, glorified is He, calmed his fear by informing him that His mercy precedes His wrath. So He said, warning and giving hope, for the sake of the denial of the deniers: ﴿Indeed﴾, and He indicated His further exaltation by mentioning the attribute of beneficence and by singling out the pronoun, so He said: ﴿your Lord﴾, meaning the One who is beneficent to you by sending you and sending down His Book to you. Whoever is honored with the like of this should not grieve over anything that occurs. ﴿Is indeed One of forgiveness﴾, meaning great in Himself, in His time and in His place, toward whomever He wills among them, so He does not decree misery for anyone.

When He encouraged them by His attribute of forgiveness, He frightened them by His attribute of retribution, and He emphasized by repeating ﴿Dhu﴾ and the waw, so He said: ﴿and Dhu punishment﴾. The closing with a rhyme letter that is the mim, together with the placing of the mim-ending name in the preceding verse, indicates the view of al-Ash'ari, who said that the verse-endings (fawasil) are not observed in the Mighty Book, and that what is relied upon is only the meanings and nothing else. The meaning here is on causing pain to those who used to pain His friends by idle talk (laghw) during the recitation (p-204), which indicates the utmost obstinacy. Therefore He placed ḥakīm first and did not say shadīd, and He said: ﴿painful﴾, meaning likewise, so He grants salvation to no one except those whom He Himself, glorified is He, has informed of their wretchedness or their deliverance. His action has already preceded in each of the two matters: He saved some people and forgave them, like the people of Jonah, upon him be peace, and He punished others. And He will do with your people from each of the two matters what is most fitting to mercy, by your sending, as indicated by the beginning of His statement with forgiveness. So the verse is like: ﴿And indeed your Lord is One of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6]. Perhaps He did not state it explicitly here out of glorification of the Qur'an, by which the discourse is connected.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 44:

When the surah opened by stating that it was sent down in the best, most beautiful, highest, clearest and most complete manner of detailed exposition, comprehensiveness and clarity, in this tongue of great station, they said about it what this consolation was given for, namely their saying ﴿Our hearts are under coverings﴾ [Fussilat: 5] to the end of the verse. Someone may have said: if it had been in a language other than Arabic, and had given this Prophet understanding of it and the ability to make it clear, it would have been stronger as a miracle and more fitting to be followed. He informed that the matter is not as they supposed, for they did not say that this doubt had arisen in them regarding his affair; rather, it was obstinacy, and the obstinate is not turned back by anything. So He said, emphatically, informing that the matter is other than what this supposer thought. Al-Asfahani said: it is an answer to their saying ﴿And they said: our hearts are under coverings﴾ [Fussilat: 5]. In my view, the best is (p-205) that it be a conjunction upon ﴿Its verses have been made distinct, an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Fussilat: 3]. It is put in the passive because it is in their tongue, so there was no need to specify who made it distinct. The sense is: We have made it Arabic and miraculous, and they are the people of knowledge of the tongue; yet they turned away from it and said what has been mentioned. The speech turned from the attribute of excellence, which required that it be Arabic, to the locus of greatness, which is the place where power is manifested and the Word is executed. ﴿And if We had made it﴾, i.e. this Reminder, with what We possess of greatness and power, ﴿a Qur'an﴾, i.e. as it is in its comprehensiveness, ﴿non-Arabic﴾, i.e. not clear in expression; and it is, together with that, in a manner suited to Our greatness, so that every person may witness that it is a miracle to non-Arabs just as this is a miracle to the Arabs, and We would have given you its understanding and the ability to make them understand it. ﴿They would have said﴾, i.e. these obstinate ones concerning it, as they say about this out of rebellion and obstinacy: ﴿Why not﴾, i.e. why not, and why does it not, ﴿its verses been made distinct﴾, i.e. been made clear in a way we can understand without hardship and without an interpreter, while being ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾ as we mentioned at the beginning of the surah.

When it became clear, by the evidence of existence and by the testimony of the Wise, the Loving, that they speak about the purely Arabic, and that they speak about the purely non-Arabic, there remained only that which is mixed from both and divided between them. So He said, resuming and disapproving of them, since it is known that this from them is merely contentiousness and not a seeking to stand upon the path of right guidance: ﴿Non-Arabic﴾ [al-Nahl: 103], i.e. is what you seek or what We seek, according to the reading of it as a statement without interrogation, non-Arabic, ﴿and Arabic﴾, made distinct in both tongues. The non-Arabic, as al-Razi said in al-Lawami', is the one who is not eloquent even if he is Arabic, and the 'ajami is one of the non-Arabs even if he speaks Arabic with eloquence.

Since it was possible for them to say: Yes, that is what we seek, and since that would be a descent from the highest rank to what is lower, although He does not answer proposed demands except for one who wants punishment, or one unable to execute what We want, He made clear that His will is executed without this. So He said: ﴿Say: it﴾, i.e. this Qur'an, in what it is of loftiness that no thing can be compared to it, ﴿is for those who believe﴾, i.e. We wished the faith to occur from them, ﴿a guidance﴾, an explanation of every sought thing, ﴿and a healing﴾ for what is in their breasts of the disease of disbelief, doubt and falsehood. Their ears are attentive to it, their hearts are receptive to it, and it is for them insights. Al-Qushayri said: it is a healing for the scholars, in that they are relieved from the toil of reflection and the bewilderment of thoughts; and a healing for the constriction of the breasts of the seekers, through the delight of reciting it and the pleasure of contemplating it; and for the hearts of the lovers, from the burning passions of (p-207) longing, through its subtle promises; and for the hearts of the knowers, through the lights of verification that follow upon them and the traces of the address of the Mighty Lord. ﴿And those who do not believe﴾, i.e. We wished that faith would not renew itself among them, ﴿in their ears is a deafness﴾, i.e. a heaviness that takes away hearing and makes one deaf. Therefore they do not hear in a way that benefits them, because they hastened to reject it the first time they heard it, and they were proud against it, so they become unable to ponder it; weakness seized them and failure deafened them, so its understanding became difficult for them. ﴿And it is for them a blindness﴾, i.e. specifically for them, a blindness that has settled over their eyes and their insights and cleaves to them, so they do not comprehend it as it should be comprehended, nor do they see the one calling to it with the sight it requires. For them there is therefore misguidance and disease. That is why they said ﴿And between us and you is a veil﴾ [Fussilat: 5]. This is because of the doubts that arise in them, for which their hearts have been prepared to accept, or because they persist in the illusions to which they are accustomed, having no attachment except to their branches and roots. It has thus become clear that the cause of the deafness in their ears is the judgment of their non-belief, since they are judged to be wretched. The verse is therefore of ihtibak (an interlocking figure): it mentioned guidance and healing first, as evidence for misguidance and disease second; and deafness and blindness second, as evidence for hearing and insights first. The secret of this is that He mentioned the most praiseworthy attributes of the believers and the most blameworthy attributes of the disbelievers, for there is nothing more contemptible than one who is deaf and blind.

When their remoteness from its loftiness and their expulsion from its precincts became clear by this, He said: ﴿Those﴾, i.e. the distant, the hateful, whose likeness is the likeness of one ﴿who is called﴾, i.e. one whom someone who wishes to call them calls, other than Allah, ﴿from a far-off place﴾. So they are in a position where their hearing is not beyond reach. As for the first group, they are called, through what they have been prepared for of acceptance, from a near place. This is the dazzling power, for one and the same thing can be in the utmost nearness for some people while for others, who are in their own place with them, it is at the utmost distance.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 45:

Since the sense is: "We have indeed given you the Book in this manner of greatness, and your community differed concerning it, as We informed you at the beginning of al-Baqarah regarding the division of people, and We punished those who were arrogant towards it by sealing upon their hearing and their hearts," he (Allah) connected to it, consoling him (the Prophet) and emphasizing for those among the People of the Book who say, in order to mislead, "If he were a prophet, people would not have differed about him," and similar things by which they confuse [the matter]: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾, i.e., by what We possess of greatness, ﴿the Book﴾, i.e., the one comprising what contains their guidance, ﴿but it was disputed﴾, i.e., disagreement occurred, ﴿concerning it﴾, i.e., among his community, just as it occurred concerning this Book, because Allah the Exalted created creation for disagreement, together with the intellects He placed in them that call to contention. ﴿And had it not been for a word﴾, i.e., a decree, ﴿that had preceded﴾ from eternity, and He turned the speech to the attribute of goodness, as a means of contentment with the decree (p-209) and consolation, and He increased that by singling Him out with the attribution, saying: ﴿from your Lord﴾, i.e., the One who is good to you, by granting success to the righteous to follow you and forsaking the wicked by casting them away from you, to relieve you of them without harm to your religion, and by leaving each one until a known term, then granting respite to all until the Day of the Supreme Decision, without annihilation by punishment as We did with other nations. ﴿The matter would have been decided﴾, i.e., the decisive judgment would have taken effect, ﴿between them﴾, the disputants, by granting the oppressed justice against his oppressor now. Since he knew by this and other [evidence] that the Day of Resurrection has been decreed by Him and made an appointed time, with the One before whom the word is not changed, it became clear that it is unavoidable and there is no escape from it, while they dispute about it. He said, emphasizing: ﴿And indeed they are in disquieting doubt﴾, i.e., encompassing them, ﴿concerning it﴾, i.e., the judgment of the Day of Decision, ﴿disquieting﴾, i.e., causing unease and suspicion, in such a way that they are not able to escape its circle at all.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 46:

Since it has been established by what preceded that the obedient one is saved, and it has been made clear that the disobedient one is ruined, the outcome follows without any doubt: ﴿Whoever does righteousness﴾, whether male or female, ﴿it is for his own soul﴾, i.e., his deed benefits it by its blessing, and it does not extend beyond it. The soul (nafs) is in need of purification through righteous deeds, since it is the locus of deficiencies; therefore it is expressed by it. The standard form of expression would have been on the side of righteousness. ﴿And whoever does evil﴾ — this conveys the shift to what is expressed, together with mentioning the deed first, whose foundation is knowledge: that the righteous deed's validity depends on its intention, and that the evil deed is held against its doer, in general, by Allah or by people, even if it occurred by error. Therefore He said: ﴿and whoever does evil﴾ (p-210), i.e., in his deed, ﴿it is against it﴾, i.e., against his own soul specifically; nothing of it falls upon anyone else.

Since the purpose of the surah has a great focus on mercy, He, glory be to Him, frequently repeated the attribute of Lordship in it. So He said, connecting to what is implied: "Your Lord does not abandon the recompense of anyone at all, whether good or evil": ﴿And your Lord is not⁠ ⁠﴾, i.e., the Benefactor to you by sending you to complete the noble traits of character. Since it is not valid at all, nor conceivable, that injustice be attributed to Him, glory be to Him, He expressed, to indicate this, with an indefinite noun in the context of negation, indicating the attribution, linked with the preposition, so He said: ﴿to the slightly wronged⁠ ⁠﴾, i.e., with any wrong ﴿to the servants⁠ ⁠﴾, i.e., the species. So it is not conceivable that any injustice would proceed from Him to anyone at all, because He has absolute independence and perfect wisdom. He expressed it with "ʿabīd" rather than "ʿibād," because it is a place of compassion and informing of weakness and lack of ability to defend oneself, and of obstinacy that indicates obedience and not contemptibility; rather, honoring this is the most common usage. Perhaps the wisdom of expressing it in the form of intensification (ẓallām) is the indication that if He were to leave off judgment and the taking of the wronged from the wrongdoer, He would be extremely unjust in terms of abandoning wisdom, which is placing things in their most perfect places, and then in terms of placing a thing in a place other than its own, which is pardoning the offender and abandoning support for the wronged in a non-appropriate place, and in terms of equating the doer of good with the doer of evil. That is more severe in threatening the wrongdoer, because the Wise does not oppose wisdom, so how much more so when the opposition is at the furthest extreme from it. This, moreover, does not harm the expression (p-211), because it is also laid down for the attribution to the basic meaning absolutely, and because the negation of absolute injustice is explicitly stated in other verses.

The preceding verse included the recompense for every great and small deed, every little and much, and the clearing of God from injustice, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And judgment will be passed between them with truth, and they will not be wronged﴾ [39:69], ﴿and every soul will be paid in full for what it did﴾ [39:70], ﴿and He is most knowing of what they do﴾ [39:70]. It also pointed to the threat of recompense on the Day of Distinction (yawm al-fasl), because we see that most of creation dies without recompense. It was their habit to ask about the knowledge of that Day. Abandoning recompense happens only through incapacity, and injustice happens only through ignorance, since injustice is placing things in other than their proper places, like the act of one walking in darkness. So He indicated His exaltedness above both of these by His perfect knowledge, which entails the comprehensiveness of power, in a way that contains their answer to the question about the knowledge of the time when the Hour will arise. This was the reason for the revelation of this verse, as Ibn al-Jawzi mentioned. He said, by way of explanation: (p-212) ﴿To Him﴾, that is, to the One who does good to you and not to anyone else, ﴿is referred﴾ by every referrer ﴿the knowledge of the Hour﴾, that is, the Hour which, in truth, is the only real "Hour", because of the matters it contains, to which nothing else bears any relation. Thus it is the one present in all minds for this. Recompense for evil and good will take place in it, so that it becomes manifestly clear to everyone that there is no injustice at all. Therefore no one other than Him can be asked about it, nor can anyone inform about it in a way that determines its time, its manner, and its nature. Whenever the questioner moves from one who is asked to one more knowledgeable than him, he finds him like the one before him, until the matter reaches God, exalted is He. The most knowledgeable of them is the one who says: "God knows best." So His singling out of knowledge of it indicates the limit of His knowledge's reach, and His withholding it from everyone besides Him indicates the completeness of His power. The combination of the two matters entails His remoteness from injustice and that it is not valid for Him to be described by it. Therefore He must establish it, so that He pays every person with a right his right, and takes for every wronged person his due without any hardship.

Since they disputed its occurrence, let alone knowledge of it, He presented it as a established matter, settled, and mentioned what indicates the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of every event in its time, as evidence of His knowledge of what determines the time of the Hour. This is in a way that indicates His power over it and over every thing within His power, through things about which they have no dispute: the fruits of plants and the animals which (p-213) are hidden within the very things from which they emerge. These are like the emergence of people after their death from the hidden places of the earth. He said, placing sustenance before creation as is most fitting, coordinating with what is implied, namely: "So no one knows it except Him": ﴿And no fruit emerges﴾, that is, at any time, past, present, or future. The negating "mā" (the negating ما, which is only followed by the present-tense sense of verbs) enters only on the meaning of occurrence, so the intended meaning is simply the depiction of whether its time has already passed or has not yet come. He reinforced the negation with the prepositional phrase, saying: ﴿from fruits﴾, that is, small or large, suitable or unsuitable, from fruits, grains, and others. The singular in the recitation of the majority is for the genus, which is apt for the few and the many. The recitation of Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Hafs from 'Asim with the plural alerts to the multiplicity of kinds. ﴿from their sheaths﴾: the plural of kumm and kimma (both with a kasra), which is the covering of the spathe and the protection of the blossom. Anything that covers something in a complete encompassing way, when that thing is meant to emerge, is a kumm. From this comes the name for a cap, kimma, and for a shirt or similar garment, kumm. That is, nothing emerges except with His knowledge. ﴿Nor does any female conceive﴾, whether the offspring is incomplete or complete, deficient or full. Likewise the negation is repeated with the negating particle, so that it includes each individually. He used "lā" because giving birth is not like conceiving, which happens in an instant; rather, the period of waiting for it is long. So He said: ﴿nor does she give birth﴾, a child alive or dead, ﴿except﴾ while it is ﴿with His knowledge﴾, and no one other than Him has knowledge of that (p-214). Whoever claims knowledge of it should be told: the fruit of such-and-such garden, such-and-such orchard, or such-and-such town will emerge at such-and-such time, or will not produce anything at all this year; and such-and-such woman will conceive at such-and-such time and give birth at such-and-such time, or will not conceive anything this year. It is well known that no one encompasses this in knowledge except God, glorified and exalted is He.

Since His knowledge has been established explicitly and His power by necessary implication, and whoever else is incapable and ignorant of it, and since the matter of the Hour has been settled by this, namely that He is able to bring it about through the proofs He has set forth, and that it must occur because of His promise of establishing it, so that the wronged may be vindicated against his oppressor, for He is wise and does not wrong anyone, even though they dispute its establishment and deny it, He, exalted, said, depicting what the earlier context contained of their ignorance and affirming some conditions of the Resurrection, linking to what the context guided to supply, such as: "So He is powerful over everything, for He is witness over everything, and they are otherwise," affirming His power explicitly and the incapacity of the partners they claimed: ﴿And the Day He calls to them﴾, that is, the polytheists, after their resurrection from the graves, for the judgment between them in all matters. Then the One who does good to you, with all kinds of goodness, including the vindication of the wronged against his oppressor, says with reproach, rebuke, and censure: ﴿Where are My partners?﴾, that is, those you claimed would intercede for you on this Day and protect you from punishment and blame. The governing element of the adverbial phrase (p-215) is ﴿They will say﴾, that is, the polytheists: ﴿We have informed You﴾, that is, we have informed You previously through the tongue of our states and now through the tongue of our speech. In both states You are hearing that, for You hear everything that can be heard, even if no one else hears it. That is why they used the term that carries the sense of informing. ﴿None of us bears witness﴾, and they reinforced the negation by introducing the preposition into the postponed subject, saying: ﴿any witness﴾, that is, one who is living and always present, not absent, aware of what He wills without any concealment, such that nothing escapes his knowledge, so that he informs of what he informs with certainty and as a testimony. The result is that the meaning is: "We do not know any of those we used to call partners, for none of us has comprehensive knowledge."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 48:

When he had established their ignorance, he followed it with their incapacity, saying: ﴿And they will be lost﴾, that is, they will go astray, be lost, vanish and be out of sight, ﴿from them﴾. Since their objects of worship were either beings without intellect, such as idols, or were counted among them because they have no real action, he referred to them with the particle used for non-rational things, saying: ﴿what they used to﴾, that is, constantly, ﴿call upon﴾ at all times, as a matter of habit.

Since their calling upon them did not extend over the whole of the time before, he introduced the preposition, saying: ﴿before﴾. They do not see it, let alone that they would find its benefit and attain it, (p-216) as if they, given the ignorance and corruption of disposition in which they were immersed, expected to come upon them and have them intercede for them. Therefore he expressed it with the verb of supposing in His saying: ﴿and they will think﴾, that is, in that state, ﴿that there is for them﴾, and he made the negation more emphatic by introducing the preposition on the postponed subject, saying: ﴿no refuge﴾, that is, no escape, no shelter, and no way of turning away.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 49:

When their following of conjecture (ẓann) was shown even on that Day when matters are laid bare and the great decrees of what has been destined become manifest, and when they cast down their hands (in despair) on it, showing that they are in the utmost ingrained ignorance and firmly rooted in incapacity, he followed this with the proof that this is the natural disposition of this kind of creature: it is always changing in its conditions and shifting in its ways. If it is touched by good, its bulk swells and it grows haughty in pride; if it is touched by affliction, it shrinks in humiliation and becomes filled with weakness and helplessness. This is the opposite of the surah's principal aim, which is knowledge, by way of clarifying that the condition of this kind is far removed from knowledge, deeply rooted in the attributes of ignorance and evil, except for whom God protects. So He, exalted, said: ﴿Man does not tire﴾, that is, does not grow weary or impatient, ﴿of asking for good﴾, that is, of seeking it with great intensity, ﴿but if evil touches him﴾, that is, this kind, whether little or much, suddenly from a direction he does not expect, ﴿he is despairing, hopeless﴾, that is, deeply immersed in despair, which is the cutting off of hope and expectation and great grief, and the certainty that this state will persist, to the point that he becomes an example of that ﴿hopeless﴾, that is, one who dwells in the abode of the severing of hope and of wretched thoughts. Thus the second term is an emphasis of the meaning in the best and most complete manner. This is the disposition with which the species has been imprinted. Whoever among them God wills good for, He protects; and whoever God wills evil for, He lets him run with his nature, and so he becomes a disbeliever, for ﴿none despairs of God's mercy except the disbelieving people﴾. Abu Hayyan said: Yaʼs (despair) is a quality of the heart, namely that its hope of good is cut off; qunut (hopelessness) is that the traces of despair appear upon him, so that he shrinks and is broken. He began with the attribute of the heart because it is what influences what appears in outward form of brokenness.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 50:

When that showed his great ignorance and the dominance of his wretched thoughts over his reason, He followed it, as confirmation of this, with what shows that his state after this despair, in which he concluded that evil was necessary and good could not come about, is that if blessing returned to him suddenly from a direction he did not hope for, and he had no evidence of its permanence or its ending, he would revert to insolence, pride and exultation, and forget the hardship he had been in. So He said, attributing the good to Himself after He had mentioned the evil, and not attributing the evil to Himself, as a lesson in manners, expressing it with the mode of greatness (p-218), as an alert that this is part of sublime management: ﴿And if We cause him to taste﴾, i.e., the human being, whose state of being absorbed in himself has overpowered him, until it has lowered him from the rank of his fellow human beings to the rank of dumb animals, or even below them.

When the end of the previous verse described his state in the face of evil, He here placed its opposite before its complement, giving it attention, unlike what is in Surah Hud, peace be upon him. So He said: ﴿a mercy from Us﴾, i.e., a great blessing which indicates His honouring him from a direction he does not hope for. This is part of the benefit of using the particle of doubt. By affirming the preposition, it indicates the separation of this (blessing) from the harm, even though its time is close to it, so that he has combined direct experience of the three states: retribution, honour, and what lies between them, the middle position between the states of approval and wrath. Then He began to explain that, saying: ﴿after a hardship﴾, i.e., a trial and great adversity, ﴿has touched him﴾, so its burden remained upon him for a long time. He answered the oath, since it precedes the condition, with His words: ﴿he will surely say﴾, immediately upon tasting that mercy, though it may well have been a great trial, being a gradual lure (istidraj) toward ruin: ﴿This is mine﴾, i.e., this great matter belongs exclusively to me, because of my own merit, with no one sharing it with me, even though it is established and does not change, moving from the state of despair to the state of security, exultation, pride and insolence, while the time is close to the experience of trials. He forgets that it is from the bounty of God, so that he might bind it by gratitude and keep it away by disbelief. ﴿And I do not think the Hour﴾, i.e., the Resurrection, which by its greatness deserves to be specifically called the Hour, ﴿will ever come﴾, i.e., that its coming is established. Thus hope of it is cut off, whether he expresses that with his tongue or with the tongue of his state, since he acts like one who doubts it, just as the cutting off of hope of good occurs when one is engaged in evil. But here he said, by way of supposition and assumption, to ward off the one who admonishes him, on the assumption that his blessing will continue: ﴿And if I am returned﴾, i.e., on the supposition, by some compelling force, ﴿to my Lord﴾, i.e., the One who has done good to me with this good in which I am, ﴿surely I shall have with Him﴾ and he emphasised it against the one who admonishes him, saying that He will punish him if he does not do well in heart and body: ﴿the best﴾, i.e., a state and rank reaching such a degree of goodness that it cannot be described, because I am worthy of it, and the proof of my worthiness is the good I am in now. He forgot what he commonly observes: that many blessings are a means of gradual lure, and that many people are in the utmost blessing and then wake up with every calamity surrounding them. Thus he is between two wishes: in this world by this saying of his, and in the Hereafter he will say, "Would that I were dust" (78:40). So he remains in the impossible, and we seek refuge in God from the evil of this state.

Since this is manifest disbelief, forgetting the blessing of the Benefactor, regarding the favour as something obligatory and due, and doubting what God, glory be to Him, has declared through the tongues of all the Messengers, that it is the locus of His wisdom, He consequently said, He, glory be to Him, emphasising in response to the emphasis of this forgetful one: ﴿Then We will surely inform﴾, i.e., a great informing, with the best description, thoroughly and with justice, and He made the pronoun the description, as a clear statement of generality and an explanation of the cause that necessitates it. So He said: ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, i.e., who concealed what the intellects indicate and what clear transmitted texts require, regarding the establishing of the Hour to manifest His majesty and beauty, and that He, exalted is He, brings upon the human being both ease and hardship, so that he may fear Him, hope in Him, thank Him and call upon Him. ﴿for what they did﴾: We will not leave from it a little or a lot, small or great. So they will see it plainly, the opposite of what they supposed in the world, that they would have the best.

﴿And We shall turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [Al-Furqan: 23].

﴿And We will surely make them taste﴾, after establishing the proof against them by the full balances of justice, weighing even the weight of an atom, ﴿a severe punishment﴾ which leaves no part of their bodies or their powers untouched without encompassing it, and which their powers cannot repel.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 41, verse 51:

When he (al-Biqa'i) had explained the ignorance of man in specific states, namely his despair upon touching evil and his feeling of security upon tasting blessing after hardship, he explained his condition at blessing in general and his supplication at evil even though he was despairing, repeating it to show the alternation of his states and the contradiction of his statements and actions, expressing this in various forms so that it would be a call for him to not be too proud to return from disbelief to faith, and would remove from him the fear of doubt (p-221) through this and of being attributed to lightness and lack of steadfastness.
